message.content:
**Hydrogen – A Quick Reference to Its Key Properties**

| Category | Property | Value / Description |
|----------|----------|---------------------|
| **Basic Atomic Data** | Atomic number | 1 |
| | Atomic mass (average) | 1.008 u |
| | Electron configuration | 1s¹ |
| | Isotopes | H‑1 (protium), H‑2 (deuterium), H‑3 (tritium) |
| | Electronegativity (Pauling) | 2.20 |
| | Ionization energy | 13.598 eV (first) |
| | Electron affinity | –0.754 eV |
| | Atomic radius | ~31 pm (covalent) |
| | Van der Waals radius | ~120 pm |
| | Boiling point | –252.9 °C (−423.2 °F) at 1 atm |
| | Melting point | –259.2 °C (−434.2 °F) at 1 atm |
| | Density (gas, 0 °C, 1 atm) | 0.08988 g L⁻¹ |
| | Molar volume (ideal gas) | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ |
| | State at STP | Gas |
| | Color | Colorless |
| | Odor | Odorless |
| | Taste | Tasteless |
| | Solubility in water | ~1.6 g L⁻¹ (≈0.18 mol L⁻¹) |
| | Solubility in organic solvents | Good in many (e.g., ethanol, acetone) |
| | pH of aqueous solution | ~7 (neutral) |
| | Dielectric constant | ~1.3 (gas) |
| | Magnetic moment | 1 µB (free atom) |
| | Spin | ½ (proton) |
| | Nuclear spin | ½ (protium), 0 (deuterium), ½ (tritium) |
| **Physical Properties** | Boiling point (under 1 atm) | –252.9 °C |
| | Melting point (under 1 atm) | –259.2 °C |
| | Density (liquid, 20 °C) | 0.0708 g cm⁻³ |
| | Density (solid, 0 K) | 0.0708 g cm⁻³ (α‑phase) |
| | Specific heat (gas, 25 °C) | 28.836 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ |
| | Thermal conductivity (gas, 25 °C) | 0.180 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ |
| | Electrical conductivity (gas) | Very low (non‑metallic) |
| | Refractive index (gas, 589 nm) | 1.000132 |
| | Speed of sound (gas, 20 °C) | 1270 m s⁻¹ |
| **Chemical Properties** | Oxidation states | +1 (most common), –1 (rare, e.g., hydride) |
| | Bonding | Forms covalent bonds (H₂, H₂O, hydrocarbons) |
| | Reactivity | Highly reactive with many elements; forms hydrides with metals |
| | Combustion | 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O (exothermic, ΔH ≈ –286 kJ mol⁻¹) |
| | Acid–base behavior | Acts as a weak acid (HF) or base (H₂O) depending on context |
| | Redox behavior | Can be oxidized to H⁺ (in acids) or reduced to H₂ (in electrolytes) |
| | Isotopic chemistry | Deuterium and tritium form heavier analogues (D₂, T₂) with slightly different bond strengths |
| | Spectroscopy | Strong absorption in UV (Lyman series), IR (stretching of H–H bond) |
| | Catalytic behavior | Used as a reducing agent in hydrogenation reactions |
| **Isotopic Variants** | Protium (¹H) | Stable, most abundant |
| | Deuterium (²H) | Stable, 0.015% natural abundance |
| | Tritium (³H) | Radioactive (half‑life ≈ 12.32 y), used in nuclear fusion research |
| **Applications & Significance** | Energy carrier | Hydrogen fuel cells, rocket propellant |
| | Industrial uses | Production of ammonia (Haber process), methanol, hydrogenation of fats |
| | Scientific research | Standard for mass spectrometry, calibration of instruments |
| | Environmental impact | Clean combustion (water only) but production often carbon‑intensive |

---

### Quick Takeaways

- **Lightest element**: Hydrogen is the simplest atom, with one proton and one electron.
- **Highly reactive**: It readily forms bonds with almost all other elements, especially oxygen and nitrogen.
- **Energy‑dense**: In terms of mass, hydrogen stores the most energy per unit mass (though its volumetric energy density is low).
- **Isotopic diversity**: The presence of stable deuterium and radioactive tritium gives hydrogen unique nuclear and chemical properties.
- **Key role in life**: Hydrogen atoms are central to organic molecules, water, and biochemical processes.

Feel free to ask if you’d like deeper details on any specific property or application!
